explanation.title: Spanish Register & Formality: Speaking Appropriately in Different Contexts

sections.subtitle: Tú vs Usted: Informal vs Formal You
sections.content: Spanish has two ways to say 'you' (singular): TÚ (informal) and USTED (formal). TÚ: Used with friends, family, children, peers, casual situations. 'Tú hablas español' (You speak Spanish - informal). Conjugates with second person singular forms. USTED: Used with strangers, elders, authority figures, professional contexts, showing respect. 'Usted habla español' (You speak Spanish - formal). Conjugates with THIRD PERSON singular (like él/ella), even though it means 'you'. This is crucial! 'Tú tienes' (you have - informal) vs 'Usted tiene' (you have - formal, third person conjugation). WHEN TO USE TÚ: With friends, classmates, siblings, children, people your age in casual settings, after someone suggests 'Háblame de tú' (Speak to me informally). WHEN TO USE USTED: With elderly people, professors, doctors, bosses, police officers, in stores/restaurants initially, when meeting someone for the first time (especially if older or in professional context). REGIONAL VARIATION: Latin America tends to use usted more than Spain. In Spain, tú is common even with strangers in informal contexts. Some regions use VOS instead of tú. SWITCHING: People may suggest switching: 'Podemos tutearnos' (We can use tú with each other). Once established, maintain consistency. When in doubt, start formal (usted) and wait for cues to switch to tú.

sections.subtitle: Vosotros vs Ustedes: Plural You in Spain vs Latin America
sections.content: PLURAL 'YOU': Spanish has regional differences. SPAIN uses two forms: VOSOTROS/VOSOTRAS (informal plural you) and USTEDES (formal plural you). LATIN AMERICA uses only USTEDES for both formal and informal plural you. VOSOTROS/AS (Spain only - informal): Used when addressing multiple people informally (friends, family). 'Vosotros habláis español' (You all speak Spanish - informal plural in Spain). Conjugates with second person plural forms ending in -áis, -éis, -ís. 'Vosotros tenéis' (you all have), 'Vosotros vivís' (you all live). USTEDES (formal in Spain, all contexts in Latin America): Uses THIRD PERSON PLURAL conjugation (like ellos/ellas), even though it means 'you all'. 'Ustedes hablan español' (You all speak Spanish - formal in Spain, general in Latin America). 'Ustedes tienen' (you all have - third person plural even though it means 'you'). IN SPAIN: Vosotros with friends/family, ustedes with strangers/formal contexts. 'Vosotros sois mis amigos' (You are my friends - informal). 'Ustedes son muy amables' (You are very kind - formal). IN LATIN AMERICA: Only ustedes used, regardless of formality level. 'Ustedes son mis amigos' (You are my friends - using ustedes but informal situation). NO VOSOTROS in Latin America except in very formal writing or religious texts. When learning, know your target region!

sections.subtitle: Formal Imperatives: Commands with Usted/Ustedes
sections.content: COMMANDS (imperatives) change form based on formality. INFORMAL (TÚ) commands use different forms. FORMAL commands with USTED/USTEDES use SUBJUNCTIVE forms. TÚ COMMANDS (informal): Affirmative = special forms (often third person singular). 'Habla' (Speak!), 'Come' (Eat!), 'Vive' (Live!). Negative = present subjunctive. 'No hables' (Don't speak!), 'No comas' (Don't eat!). USTED COMMANDS (formal): Both affirmative and negative use present subjunctive forms. 'Hable (usted)' (Speak! - formal), 'Coma' (Eat! - formal), 'Viva' (Live! - formal). Negative: 'No hable' (Don't speak - formal), 'No coma' (Don't eat - formal). USTEDES COMMANDS (formal in Spain, all in Latin America): Use present subjunctive plural. 'Hablen (ustedes)' (Speak! - plural formal), 'Coman' (Eat! - plural), 'No hablen' (Don't speak - plural). VOSOTROS COMMANDS (informal plural, Spain only): Affirmative = infinitive with -d. 'Hablad' (Speak! - you all), 'Comed' (Eat!), 'Vivid' (Live!). Negative = present subjunctive. 'No habléis' (Don't speak! - vosotros). POLITENESS IN COMMANDS: Add 'por favor' (please). 'Hable más despacio, por favor' (Speak more slowly, please - formal). Common formal commands: 'Pase' (Come in), 'Siéntese' (Sit down), 'Dígame' (Tell me / How can I help you?), 'Disculpe' (Excuse me).

sections.subtitle: Politeness Strategies: Conditional & Subjunctive
sections.content: Beyond tú/usted, Spanish uses various strategies to sound polite and soften requests. CONDITIONAL for polite requests: Instead of direct statements, use conditional to sound less demanding. Direct: '¿Puedes ayudarme?' (Can you help me? - informal). Polite: '¿Podrías ayudarme?' (Could you help me? - conditional, softer). '¿Querrías venir?' (Would you want to come? - more polite than quieres). 'Me gustaría hablar contigo' (I would like to talk to you - softer than quiero). SUBJUNCTIVE with QUISIERA (imperfect subjunctive of querer): Very polite way to make requests. 'Quisiera un café, por favor' (I would like a coffee, please - very polite, more than quiero). 'Quisiera hacer una pregunta' (I would like to ask a question - polite). PODER (could/can): 'Podría' (conditional) more polite than 'puede'. '¿Podría ayudarme?' (Could you help me? - formal, very polite). INDIRECT QUESTIONS more polite: 'Me pregunto si podrías...' (I wonder if you could...). '¿Te importaría...?' (Would you mind...?). PERMISSION: '¿Podría pasar?' (Could I come in? - polite). '¿Le importa si...?' (Do you mind if...? - formal). DIMINUTIVES for politeness: 'Un momentito' (just a little moment - softer than momento). 'Un cafecito' (a little coffee - friendlier). EXPRESSIONS: 'Si no es molestia' (if it's not a bother), 'Cuando puedas' (whenever you can), 'Si fuera/fuese posible' (if it were possible).

sections.subtitle: More Politeness: Expressions & Avoiding Directness
sections.content: AVOIDING DIRECT STATEMENTS: Spanish values indirect communication in polite contexts. Instead of direct negatives, use softeners. Direct: 'No puedo' (I can't). Softer: 'Me temo que no puedo' (I'm afraid I can't), 'Lamentablemente no puedo' (Unfortunately I can't). Instead of 'No': 'Es que...' (It's just that... - excuse/explanation), 'Es que no tengo tiempo' (It's just that I don't have time - softer refusal). APOLOGETIC: 'Disculpe/Perdone' (Excuse me/Pardon me - formal), 'Perdona/Disculpa' (Sorry - informal). 'Siento molestar' (I'm sorry to bother), 'Perdone que le interrumpa' (Pardon me for interrupting - formal). MAKING REQUESTS: Frame as questions rather than commands. Instead of 'Dame el libro' (Give me the book - direct), use '¿Me das el libro?' (Will you give me the book?), '¿Me darías el libro?' (Would you give me the book? - conditional), '¿Podrías darme el libro?' (Could you give me the book? - very polite). RESPONDING POLITELY: To thanks: 'De nada' (You're welcome), 'No hay de qué' (Don't mention it), 'Con mucho gusto' (With pleasure). To requests: 'Con mucho gusto' (With pleasure), 'Por supuesto' (Of course), 'Cómo no' (Of course/Why not - Latin America). DECLINING POLITELY: 'Muchas gracias, pero...' (Thank you very much, but...), 'Te lo agradezco, pero...' (I appreciate it, but...). These strategies show cultural competence beyond just grammar.

sections.subtitle: Register-Appropriate Vocabulary & Situations
sections.content: REGISTER refers to language formality level appropriate for different situations. INFORMAL REGISTER (friends, family): Use tú, vosotros (in Spain), colloquial vocabulary, contractions, slang. 'Tío/Tía' (dude - Spain slang), 'Vale' (OK - Spain), '¿Qué onda?' (What's up? - Mexico), 'Chévere' (Cool - Latin America). Can omit subject pronouns, use incomplete sentences. NEUTRAL REGISTER (everyday interactions): Clear, standard Spanish. Use usted with strangers initially. Correct grammar, everyday vocabulary. In stores, restaurants, with acquaintances. 'Buenos días, ¿cómo está?' (Good morning, how are you? - neutral/formal). FORMAL REGISTER (professional, academic, official): Always usted/ustedes. Complete sentences, precise vocabulary, subjunctive used correctly, no slang. 'Me gustaría solicitar información' (I would like to request information - formal). 'Le agradezco su atención' (I thank you for your attention - formal). Business emails: 'Estimado/a señor/a' (Dear Sir/Madam), 'Atentamente' (Sincerely). ACADEMIC: Passive voice more common, complex structures. 'Se llevó a cabo un estudio' (A study was carried out - formal/academic). VERY FORMAL/LITERARY: 'Vuestra merced' (Your grace - archaic, origin of usted). Religious: Vos forms in liturgy. REGIONAL VARIATIONS: Vocabulary choices signal register and region. 'Coche' (car - Spain) vs 'Carro/Auto' (car - Latin America). Choose appropriate register for context - using too informal register in formal situations shows lack of cultural awareness.

questions.question: When do you use TÚ?

answers.text: With friends, family, children, peers (informal contexts)

questions.hint: TÚ = informal. Use with friends, family, peers in casual situations.

questions.question: When do you use USTED?

answers.text: With strangers, elders, authority figures, professional contexts

questions.hint: USTED = formal. Use to show respect with strangers, elders, professionals.

questions.question: 'Tú hablas' vs 'Usted habla' - Why different verb forms?

answers.text: Usted uses third person conjugation even though it means 'you'

questions.hint: Key rule: USTED conjugates like él/ella (third person), not like tú (second person).

questions.question: 'Tú tienes' formally becomes...
questions.hint: USTED uses third person: tiene (like él/ella tiene), not tienes.

questions.question: In doubt, which form should you start with?

answers.text: USTED (formal) - wait for cues to switch to tú

questions.hint: When uncertain, start formal (USTED) and wait for the other person to suggest tú.

questions.question: Which form is used in SPAIN for informal plural 'you'?
questions.hint: Spain uses VOSOTROS for informal plural you (you all - friends/family).

questions.question: Which form is used in LATIN AMERICA for plural 'you' (all contexts)?
questions.hint: Latin America ONLY uses USTEDES for plural you (formal and informal contexts).

questions.question: 'Vosotros habláis' vs 'Ustedes hablan' - What's the pattern?

answers.text: Vosotros = 2nd person plural; Ustedes = 3rd person plural conjugation

questions.hint: VOSOTROS = 2nd person plural (habláis). USTEDES = 3rd person plural (hablan, like ellos).

questions.question: Is VOSOTROS used in Mexico?

answers.text: No - Latin America only uses ustedes

questions.hint: VOSOTROS is Spain only. Latin America (including Mexico) uses USTEDES for all plural you.

questions.question: Formal command (usted): 'Hablar' (to speak) becomes...
questions.hint: USTED commands use present subjunctive: Hable (usted) = Speak! (formal).

questions.question: Formal negative command: 'Don't speak' (usted) is...
questions.hint: Formal commands (affirmative and negative) use subjunctive: No hable.

questions.question: Informal affirmative command (tú): 'Come' means...
questions.hint: Come = Eat! (informal tú command). Context determines if command or indicative.

questions.question: Common formal command meaning 'Come in':
questions.hint: PASE (usted) = Come in! (formal). Very common in shops, offices.

questions.question: '¿Puedes ayudarme?' vs '¿Podrías ayudarme?' - Which is more polite?
questions.hint: CONDITIONAL (podrías = could you?) is more polite than present (puedes = can you?).

questions.question: 'Quisiera un café' - What does quisiera express?
questions.hint: QUISIERA (imperfect subjunctive of querer) = I would like (very polite, softer than quiero).

questions.question: '¿Podría ayudarme?' vs '¿Puede ayudarme?' - Which is more polite?
questions.hint: PODRÍA (conditional) = could you? More polite/softer than PUEDE (can you?).

questions.question: 'Me temo que no puedo' vs 'No puedo' - Which is more polite?

answers.text: Me temo que no puedo (I'm afraid I can't - softer)

questions.hint: Softeners like 'Me temo que' (I'm afraid that) make refusals more polite and indirect.

questions.question: 'Es que no tengo tiempo' - What does 'Es que' do?

answers.text: Makes it more direct and forceful

questions.hint: ES QUE = It's just that... (softener for excuses/refusals, less direct than blunt 'no').

questions.question: Instead of 'Dame el libro' (Give me the book), more polite is...

answers.text: ¿Podrías darme el libro? (Could you give me...?)
Dame el libro ahora (Give me the book now)

questions.hint: Frame as polite question with conditional: ¿Podrías...? (Could you...?) instead of direct command.

questions.question: Response to 'Gracias' (Thank you):

answers.text: De nada / No hay de qué (You're welcome / Don't mention it)

questions.hint: DE NADA or NO HAY DE QUÉ = You're welcome (standard responses to thanks).

questions.question: Which is INFORMAL register vocabulary?

answers.text: Me gustaría solicitar (I would like to request)

questions.hint: Informal register uses slang and colloquialisms: Tío, Vale, ¿Qué onda?, Chévere.

questions.question: Which is FORMAL register for business email?
questions.hint: Formal email: Estimado/a (Dear), Atentamente (Sincerely), Le agradezco (I thank you).

questions.question: What does appropriate REGISTER mean?

answers.text: Matching formality level to the situation/context
Always using the most formal Spanish
Always using slang to sound natural

questions.hint: REGISTER = formality level appropriate for context. Informal with friends, formal at work, neutral in shops.

questions.question: 'Disculpe' vs 'Disculpa' - What's the difference?

answers.text: Disculpe is formal (usted); Disculpa is informal (tú)
Disculpe is plural; Disculpa is singular
Both are exactly the same formality

questions.hint: DISCULPE (usted command) = Excuse me (formal). DISCULPA (tú command) = Excuse me (informal).
